A2.text:
Nigar is ten. Her cousin, Farid, is fourteen. Every Friday, the family has dinner at their grandfather's house. After dinner, Nigar and Farid play chess.

Farid always wins. But Farid is not a fair opponent. When Nigar looks away, he moves her pieces. He likes to cheat. Nigar cries, and sometimes she wants to give up.

One day, her grandfather, Tofig, said, “Come here. I will teach you a strategy.”

Every evening, Nigar and her grandfather played chess on the phone. The game was addictive. Nigar played every day. Her grandfather gave her a clue: “Watch his face. When he smiles, he has a plan. But you must keep a poker face. Never show your plan.”

On Friday, Nigar played Farid again. When it was Farid's turn, he moved her horse. But this time Nigar saw it.

“Put it back,” she said calmly. Farid was surprised.

The first game was a draw. In the second game, Nigar did not smile. She kept a poker face. Farid did not understand her plan. Then Nigar said, “Checkmate.”

Farid looked at the board. He could not believe it.

Grandfather Tofig laughed. “You can beat someone at their own game,” he said, “if you play your cards right.”

B1.text:
Every Friday, the whole family gathered for dinner at Grandfather Tofig's house in Mardakan, and every Friday ended the same way: ten-year-old Nigar sitting at the chessboard opposite her cousin Farid, fourteen, and losing.

Farid wasn't just a strong opponent. He was a cheat. Whenever Nigar turned to take a sip of her juice, one of her pieces would mysteriously move to a worse square. She complained, he laughed, the adults told them to stop arguing, and Nigar went home close to tears, ready to give up chess forever.

One evening her grandfather took her aside. “Losing is fine,” he said. “Losing to a cheat is not. Let's work on your strategy.”

For the next two months, they played every evening on a chess app, Tofig on his tablet in Mardakan, Nigar on her mother's phone in the city. The app was surprisingly addictive; Nigar started solving puzzles on the bus to school. Her grandfather also gave her a clue that had nothing to do with chess. “Watch Farid's face. When he's planning something, his ears go red. And you — never let him read yours. You need a poker face.”

The following Friday, Nigar sat down at the board as usual. When it was Farid's turn, she pretended to look away, and out of the corner of her eye she saw his hand move her knight.

“Put it back, please,” she said without looking up.

Farid's ears turned bright red.

Their first game ended in a draw, which had never happened before. In the second, Nigar played slowly and silently, her face as calm as a lake. Farid kept glancing at her, trying to guess what she was thinking. He couldn't. Twenty minutes later, she quietly moved her queen.

“Checkmate.”

The room went silent. Farid stared at the board as if it had betrayed him.

From his armchair, Grandfather Tofig raised his tea glass. “It's possible to beat someone at their own game,” he said, “if you play your cards right.”

B2.text:
Friday dinners at Grandfather Tofig's house in Mardakan followed a ritual as fixed as the tides: plov, an argument about politics, tea under the fig tree — and ten-year-old Nigar being dismantled at chess by her fourteen-year-old cousin Farid.

The humiliation had less to do with Farid's talent than with his methods. He was an unashamed cheat. Whenever Nigar turned to reach for her juice, a piece of hers would quietly migrate to a hopeless square. She would protest; he would grin; some adult would tell them both to stop squabbling. Nigar regularly went home on the verge of tears, half determined to give up the game for good.

One evening, Tofig steered her onto the veranda. “Losing is perfectly respectable,” he said. “Losing to a cheat is not. We're going to work on your strategy.”

For two months they played every night on an app — he on his tablet in Mardakan, she on her mother's phone across the city. The thing proved fiendishly addictive; Nigar took to solving puzzles on the bus to school. Her grandfather also slipped her a clue that had nothing to do with the rules of chess. “Study your opponent, not just the board. When Farid is about to try something, the tips of his ears turn red. As for you — he must never be able to read your face. Learn a poker face.”

The next Friday, Nigar took her usual seat. When it was Farid's turn, she made a show of gazing out of the window, and from the corner of her eye watched his fingers drift towards her knight.

“Put that back, please,” she said, without turning her head.

The tips of Farid's ears glowed crimson.

Their first game ended in a draw — unprecedented in the family's history. The second she played slowly and in total silence, her expression as untroubled as a frozen pond. Farid's eyes kept flicking from the board to her face and back, searching for a hint. There was none. Twenty minutes in, she slid her queen diagonally across the board.

“Checkmate.”

The veranda fell silent. Farid gazed at the pieces as though they had personally conspired against him.

From the depths of his armchair, Grandfather Tofig lifted his tea glass in salute. “You see? You can beat someone at their own game,” he remarked, “provided you play your cards right.”

podcast.title: Nard in the yard

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: What games do you play? Guess: who in Leyla's family cheats at cards?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is games and puzzles. Leyla, I have news: I've started playing nard.
Backgammon! Who taught you?
Mr Aliyev, your neighbour. He plays in the yard every evening.
[laugh] Then you're losing every game.
Every single one. He has a perfect poker face. I never know what he's thinking.
And he plays fast. Before you finish your turn, he's already moving.
Yes! And he talks about strategy the whole time — in Azerbaijani. I understand nothing.
Did you ever win?
Once it was a draw. Well, we stopped because it got dark. [chuckle]
In my family the big game is cards at New Year. And my grandmother always cheats.
Your grandmother? No!
She hides cards in her sleeve. We all know, but nobody says anything.
[laugh] That's a clever opponent.
What about puzzles? Do you like them?
Crosswords. Every Sunday with my coffee. But some clues are impossible.
Do you give up?
Never. I put it on the fridge and finish it on Wednesday.
My niece Aysu plays a puzzle game on her phone. It's so addictive — she plays it under the table at dinner.
Ah, the modern way to hide cards in your sleeve.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: what game are you really good at — and do you play to win or just for fun?
I play to win. I just don't win yet. See you next time!
Bye for now!
